title: Weibull arrival queueing sim - scratch
body:
Goal:
Quick personal sim notes exploring how non-Poisson (Weibull) arrival processes change tail latency under different batching/timeouts and small-service-time regimes. Trying to surface heuristics that are easy to add to the runtime (adaptive batch timeouts, small prefetch pools).

Motivation:
- We see customer traces that are bursty but not pure Poisson; many have heavy tails in inter-arrival times (bursty sessions) that degrade p99/p999 even when p95 looks fine.
- Prior experiments (poisson-arrival-sweep) assumed Poisson. Need to understand sensitivity to shape parameter (k) and how batching/timeouts interact.

Experiment plan (fast sim, event-driven):
- Arrival process: Weibull(k, lambda) with k in {0.6, 1.0, 1.5}.
  - k=1 -> exponential (Poisson arrivals) baseline.
  - k<1 -> heavy-tailed clustering (more short gaps + long idle periods).
  - k>1 -> more regular arrivals (less variance).
- Service time: deterministic-ish with small jitter: base = 10ms per token-chunk (service unit), add Exp(1/2ms) jitter.
- Batching model: server accepts requests and forms batches up to batch_max_size (S) or until batch_timeout (T) elapses, whichever first. Batch service time scales sublinearly: service(batch_size) = 10ms + 0.9 * 10ms * (batch_size-1) (toy model).
- Concurrency: single GPU worker (M=1), examine client concurrency (0.5x, 1x, 2x of base throughput).
- Metrics captured: qps, util, p50/p95/p99/p999 queue+service latency, batch size distribution, fraction of requests served by timeout vs full batch.

Sim parameters (swept):
- k = 0.6, 1.0, 1.5
- batch_max_size S = 1, 4, 8
- batch_timeout T = 2ms, 5ms, 10ms
- offered load: set so that Poisson case (k=1) sits at ~70% util for baseline (safe area)

Quick implementation notes:
- Event-driven sim, priority queue for arrival+completion events.
- Use 20M simulated requests per run for stable tail stats. Shorter runs (2M) are OK for quick iteration.
- Keep random seed fixed per experiment for repeatability.

Representative results (toy numbers, aggregated):
- Baseline (k=1, S=8, T=10ms): util=68%, p50=14ms, p95=42ms, p99=86ms, p999=210ms, mean batch size=6.8, timeout_served=12%
- Heavy tail (k=0.6, S=8, T=10ms): util=70%, p50=16ms, p95=78ms, p99=220ms, p999=980ms, mean batch size=4.1, timeout_served=34%
- Regular (k=1.5, S=8, T=10ms): util=65%, p50=12ms, p95=28ms, p99=48ms, p999=110ms, mean batch size=7.5, timeout_served=5%

Observations:
- Heavy-tailed arrivals massively inflate the extreme tails (p999) even at modest util levels. Poisson-based benchmarks understate worst-case tail by 3-5x in this sim.
- Mean batch size drops for k<1 because arrivals cluster and then gap, so many batches are cutoff by timeout when gaps appear. That increases per-request latency for those arriving in low-cluster windows.
- Increasing batch_timeout T reduces tail but increases average latency. There is a sweet spot (application-dependent): e.g., T=5ms gave better p99 than T=2ms for k=0.6 while keeping p50 relatively stable.
- Smaller S (batch_max) reduces p999 slightly (less queuing behind big batches) but hurts throughput efficiency.

Mini sensitivity table (excerpts):
- k=0.6 (heavy):
  - S=8,T=2ms -> p99=310ms, p999 ~1200ms
  - S=8,T=10ms -> p99=220ms, p999 ~980ms
  - S=4,T=5ms -> p99=260ms, p999 ~1050ms (tradeoff)
- k=1.5 (regular): differences small across T; p999 stays <150ms if util <75%

Heuristics worth trying in runtime (low-effort):
1) Adaptive batch timeout: if recent inter-arrival variance > threshold (observed burst/gap pattern), reduce T during gaps and increase T during densest windows. Implement as EWMA of inter-arrival gaps per route or token-class.
2) Small pre-warming pool for cold windows: keep 1-2 warm workers that accept small batches with smaller T to avoid long tail when a cluster of requests comes after a long idle. Cost small but reduces p999 for k<1.
3) Emergency fast-path: if request has hard SLO tag, bypass batching (S=1) or go to low-latency pool.
4) Per-tenant arrival-shape detectors: track shape metric (simple variance/skew) and pick policy (batching params) per-tenant/route.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Validate against real production traces (ask SRE/Telemetry for 24h traces from 3 customers with bursty patterns).
- Replace toy batch-service scaling with measured kernel scaling from benchmarking (how service time grows with batch size on A100/4H100).
- Explore mixed workloads: mix large-service requests (long running) and short ones to see head-of-line blocking effects.
- Add key-value cache hit correlation: if repeated queries hit KV cache, they should be fast and reduce effective service time — how does that interact with Weibull arrivals?
- Quick follow-up: run the same sims but vary util from 40% to 90% to map region where tails blow up for k<1.

Notes to self (implementation checklist):
- [ ] Commit sim harness to runtime/utils/sim (single-file, ~300 LOC), paramized YAML for sweeps.
- [ ] Wire in lib to parse real trace CSVs (ts, tenant, size) and fit Weibull k via MLE.
- [ ] Add plotting helper for tail-quantile vs T,S heatmaps.
- [ ] Share draft with Maya + SRE next week (put on Opt-Bench Slack channel).

Quick conclusion (for design doc):
- Don’t assume Poisson. Heavy-tailed inter-arrivals are common and significantly worsen extreme tails even when stable throughput metrics look fine. Reasonable runtime controls (adaptive T, tiny pre-warm pools, route-level policies) can mitigate p999 without sacrificing much throughput.

Log/versions: sim v0.1 (fast), seed=42, run_id=weibull-k-sweep-20241210

Raw sample ascii chart (p99 vs k for S=8,T=5ms):
k    | p99 (ms)
0.6  | 260
1.0  | 86
1.5  | 48

If this holds up on traces, propose a small RFC: "adaptive-batch-timeouts-by-arrival-shape" (10-12pt RFC, include cost/benefit and perf sims).

End of scratchpad.
